extracted.intended_audience: general readers of 19th-century social essays; readers interested in gambling, card-games, and social commentary
extracted.subtask_description: Expository essay describing American and European gambling practices, rules and strategies for several card games, methods of cheating, and social consequences—aimed at informing and critiquing gambling culture. Includes procedural descriptions of how games are played and how gamblers/house-proprietors behave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing professional vs ordinary gambler
rubrics_metrics.description: At American gambling houses 'it is very easy ... to distinguish the professional from the ordinary gambler.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary gambler: 'a nervous expression about the mouth, and an intense gaze upon the cards, and altogether a very serious nervous appearance.' Professional: 'plays in a very quiet manner, and seems to care but little how the game goes; and his desire to appear as if the game was new to him is almost certain to expose him to those who know the manoeuvre.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw Poker (Bluff) — dealing, betting order, and the blind
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for Draw Poker: dealer determined by fixing on a card; dealer posts an Ante; five cards dealt to each player; the player next to dealer may stake a 'blind' before looking at cards, making him elder hand/last player.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blind may be abandoned by giving up the first stake; if not abandoned it becomes the elder hand; any player (before looking) may raise on the blind; if no intervening player meets the blind it must be made good by all who wish to play and the last player must make good the full amount. Every player except the blind may look at his cards in his turn before deciding to meet the blind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw Poker — hand rankings and relative values
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative value of hands given: four of a kind (four aces best) > full (three of a kind + pair) > flush (five cards of one colour) > threes (three of a kind) > sequence (straight) > two pairs > one pair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains examples and that a flush of five same-colour cards ranks above threes and below full; sequences need not be same colour unless they form a flush.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw Poker — drawing strategy: 'to know what to throw away'
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategic maxim for drawing: the primary skill is to 'know what to throw away' to induce other players to improve the hand or to maximize your own improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: if you have a pair throw away three cards; with threes some players throw away two odd cards to try for four of a kind or at least a full; some will 'stand out' (not draw) to deceive others into thinking they have a straight or flush. Players use demeanor (calm, chatter, badinage, studying cards, gazing) to disguise the real hand and influence betting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw Poker — betting process and show-of-hands closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Betting proceeds after drawing; blind/first better leads and may bet small to entice others to raise; a player's first bet does not preclude additional betting if later raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the original bet goes round back to the blind without anyone 'going better' the game closes and becomes a 'show of hands' to determine the winner; some players will throw cards among the waste and abandon stakes to conceal method or when bluffing fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poker (no-draw) variant — structure and player limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Pokers differs in that players receive only the original five cards dealt without drawing new ones and must either play or refuse on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because there are more cards in play in this variant, as many as ten persons can play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lansquenet — banker stakes and matching-card win condition
rubrics_metrics.description: In Lansquenet the dealer/banker stakes a sum which must be met in turn by players; the dealer turns up two cards, one for himself and one for the table, then turns cards until one of them is matched — a match constitutes a win for the holder of the matched card.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the dealer's card turns up he may take the stake and pass the bank or allow the stake to remain (where it becomes doubled if met). The dealer can continue as long as cards turn in his favour and may give up the bank at any moment. When 'jumelle' (twins) occurs (similar cards on both sides) the dealer takes half the stake. The pool may be contributed to by players in proportions; terms include 'I'll see' (a moi le tout) and 'Je tiens'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lansquenet — cheating method by prepared series of cards (portees/costieres)
rubrics_metrics.description: A common card-sharper technique: preparing a series of cards (a prearranged dozen) carried in side pockets (portees/costieres) and placing them on the pack at the right moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceeding: the sharper leans negligently, seizes prepared cards from side pocket and places them on the pack. Some keep matches already dealt in costieres or hidden in the hand to lay on the pack, thereby avoiding augmentation of the pack. Example arrangement of a dozen cards is given. This is presented as an 'easy means' by which card sharpers manage long sequences of wins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euchre — deck composition, deal, and trump hierarchy (Right and Left Bowers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Euchre uses cards from seven upwards (sixes excluded); five cards dealt after shuffling with a turn-up trump; dealer may discard one card and take the trump (without showing the discarded card).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Knave (Jack) of trumps is the best card (Right Bower) and the other Knave of the same colour is the Left Bower, both ranking above other cards. If both bowers are held, the deal is usually decided since three tricks out of five secure the point. Games may be to five or seven points. Euchre is rapid and decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fly Loo — play and anti-cheating precaution
rubrics_metrics.description: Fly Loo: players place lumps of sugar before them and the player whose lump a fly first alights upon wins the pool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cheating reported: a 'cute Yankee' smeared his lump with an attractant to win invariably. Suggested preventive measure: insist upon fresh lumps of sugar and prevent touching of lumps to avoid tampering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proprietor tactics to entice customers in low-stakes gaming houses
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical proprietor behaviour in low gambling houses: employing cajoling remarks and jokes to lure patrons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of cries: 'Hallo, old sport! come and try your luck--you look lucky this evening; and if you make a good run you may sport a gold watch and chain, and a velvet vest, like myself.' Or 'Young clear-the-way, you look down at the mouth to-night! Come along and have a turn--and never mind your supper to-night.' These are presented as routine methods by which days and nights are passed in gambling houses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators and scale of gambling prevalence (for social assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported statistics and findings used to demonstrate prevalence and social impact of gambling in New York and Brooklyn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: society agents detected among gamblers 68 clerks in one month and 623 cases in six months; stated existence of 1017 policy and lottery offices and 163 Faro banks; estimated net annual gains not less than 36,000,000 dollars. Also reference to an association employing detectives who report names and occupations of those frequenting gambling rooms to subscribers (many large houses of business subscribe).
